scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that devices can hurt social skills while arguing they can also help connection; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Young people today often seem more comfortable with a screen than with the person beside them.
One claim holds that young people's heavy use of phones and tablets has hurt their social skills, on the reason that these devices encourage artificial personalities and relationships online.
I agree that devices can harm social skills, but I believe they can also help connection when used well.

sections.role: Body 1 — How devices can hurt social skills

sentences.text: First, there is real truth in the reason behind the claim.
Hours spent online can leave young people less practised at real face-to-face talk.
For example, a teenager who texts constantly may struggle to hold a live conversation.
This shows that heavy device use can weaken important social skills.
Online, people can also hide behind an artificial image of themselves rather than being honest.
Relationships built only through screens can feel thin compared with real friendship.
To this extent, the reason given for the claim has genuine force.

sections.role: Body 2 — How devices can help connection

sentences.text: Second, however, the same devices can also help young people connect.
Phones let young people stay close to friends and family they could not otherwise reach.
Consider a shy teenager who first finds the confidence to make friends through an online group.
Such cases show that devices can build social bonds rather than only weaken them.
Used wisely, technology can support real friendships instead of replacing them.
The harm comes not from the devices themselves but from using them carelessly.
Devices, then, can either hurt or help social skills depending on how they are used.
In conclusion, heavy use of phones and tablets can indeed weaken young people's social skills.
But the same devices can also help them connect when used with care.
Whether technology harms or helps social skills depends far less on the devices than on how they are used.
